content.text:
Not being able to empty your bladder completely is called **urinary retention**. It usually happens for one of two reasons: **something is blocking urine flow**, or **the bladder muscle/nerve signals aren’t working strongly enough** to push urine out. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/symptoms-causes?utm_source=openai))

Common causes include:

- **Enlarged prostate** in men — one of the most common causes, especially with age. It can squeeze the urethra and block flow. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/benign-prostatic-hyperplasia/symptoms-causes/syc-20370087?p=1&utm_source=openai))
- **Urinary tract infection or inflammation** — swelling can make it harder to pass urine. ([my.clevelandclinic.org](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/15427-urinary-retention?utm_source=openai))
- **Medications** — some cold/allergy medicines, decongestants, antihistamines, antidepressants, bladder spasm medicines, opioids, and others can interfere with bladder emptying. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/symptoms-causes?utm_source=openai))
- **Nerve problems** — diabetes, spinal cord issues, stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, or pelvic nerve injury can affect bladder signals. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/preventing-problems/sexual-bladder-problems?utm_source=openai))
- **Urethral narrowing/scar tissue** — from prior surgery, injury, infections, catheter use, or radiation.
- **Bladder stones, tumors, or masses** — can physically block urine flow.
- **Constipation** — a full rectum can press on the bladder/urethra and interfere with emptying.
- **After surgery or anesthesia** — temporary urinary retention can happen after procedures. ([yalemedicine.org](https://www.yalemedicine.org/conditions/urinary-retention?utm_source=openai))
- **Weak or underactive bladder muscle** — the bladder may fill but not squeeze well enough.

**Seek urgent care now** if you **cannot pee at all**, have a painful swollen lower belly, fever, back/flank pain, vomiting, new leg weakness/numbness, or loss of bowel control. Acute urinary retention can be serious and may need a catheter to drain the bladder.

If this is ongoing or you feel like you still have urine left after peeing, it’s worth seeing a clinician/urologist. They can check a urine test, bladder scan for “post-void residual,” prostate/pelvic exam, kidney function, and sometimes imaging or urodynamic testing.
